findings.issue_text: [Medium/bug] The new negative cache (`permDenialCache`) has no invalidation path anywhere in the diff: when a user is granted access to a previously-denied resource (or a resource is moved into a folder they can access), `Check` keeps returning `Allowed: false` from the denial entry for up to `shortCacheTTL`, even if the existing invalidation flow clears `permCache`/`idCache`. Worse, because `userPermDenialCacheKey` embeds resource name and parent folder, the per-user/per-action invalidation used for the other caches cannot target these entries at all without prefix scans.

[Medium/performance] On a perm-cache hit that evaluates to 'deny', `Check` now always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` and the cache short-circuit was removed from `getUserPermissions`, so a warm `permCache` no longer absorbs denied checks. Since the denial cache only dedups exact repeats of (user, action, name, parent), every distinct denied resource triggers a full permission-store query plus a `permCache` rewrite per TTL window, letting an authenticated client amplify DB load simply by varying `Name` (singleflight only dedups concurrent same user+action fetches).

[Medium/test_gap] The test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' (service_test.go:963) is vacuous: it seeds `permCache` with `dashboards:uid:dash1: false`, which denies on its own, and the DB fallback would also deny, so the test passes even if the denial-cache lookup were deleted entirely. The inline comment says 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked' while the code sets `false`; to actually prove the denial cache takes precedence, `permCache` must be seeded with `true` for the resource while the denial entry exists.

[Low/test_gap] There is no test that a DB-evaluated deny actually populates `permDenialCache` (i.e., that a second identical check short-circuits without re-querying the store), and no test asserts store call counts, so the write side of the new cache is completely untested.

[Low/bug] The `permissionCacheUsage` metric semantics are corrupted in `Check`: a denial-cache hit is counted as a perm-cache hit ('true') while a genuine perm-cache hit that evaluates to deny is counted as a miss ('false'). `List` reports the same metric with correct semantics, so the cache hit-rate metric now means different things per endpoint and understates real cache effectiveness for denied traffic.

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Medium/bug] The new negative cache (`permDenialCache`) has no invalidation path anywhere in the diff: when a user is granted access to a previously-denied resource (or a resource is moved into a folder they can access), `Check` keeps returning `Allowed: false` from the denial entry for up to `shortCacheTTL`, even if the existing invalidation flow clears `permCache`/`idCache`. Worse, because `userPermDenialCacheKey` embeds resource name and parent folder, the per-user/per-action invalidation used for the other caches cannot target these entries at all without prefix scans.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `permDenialCache` and makes `Check` immediately return `Allowed: false` when `s.permDenialCache.Get(...)` hits (service.go: `permDenialKey := ...; if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). The cache is populated on any DB-backed denial (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }`). Nowhere in the shown changes is `permDenialCache` ever deleted/cleared, and its key (`userPermDenialCacheKey`) includes `name` and `parent`, so any invalidation scheme that only knows `(namespace,userUID,action)` cannot address these entries without enumerating/scanning. This can cause stale false-denies until TTL expires when permissions/folder placement changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Medium/performance] On a perm-cache hit that evaluates to 'deny', `Check` now always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` and the cache short-circuit was removed from `getUserPermissions`, so a warm `permCache` no longer absorbs denied checks. Since the denial cache only dedups exact repeats of (user, action, name, parent), every distinct denied resource triggers a full permission-store query plus a `permCache` rewrite per TTL window, letting an authenticated client amplify DB load simply by varying `Name` (singleflight only dedups concurrent same user+action fetches).

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `Service.Check` only short-circuits on a cached *allow* (it returns early only when `allowed` is true). On a `permCache` hit where `checkPermission` evaluates to false, it intentionally falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (new block in `Check`), causing a permission-store fetch even with a warm `permCache`. This is reinforced by removing the cache-return paths from `getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions` (the `permCache.Get` early returns were deleted), so the only cache-read path is `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, which does not short-circuit denies. The new `permDenialCache` only avoids repeats for the exact `(namespace,user,action,name,parent)` key (`userPermDenialCacheKey`), so varying `Name`/`parent` can still trigger repeated DB permission fetches despite a warm cache. This is a concrete performance/regression concern grounded in the diff, not a correctness bug.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new write-side behavior in `Service.Check`: if a DB-evaluated check returns `!allowed`, it calls `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` (service.go). The added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`) cover (a) allow via `permCache`, (b) DB fallback on cache miss/outdated cache, and (c) deny when `permDenialCache` is pre-populated — but none exercise the path where the first request is denied via DB and then verify that a second identical request is short-circuited by the newly written `permDenialCache` entry. Also, none of the tests assert store/query invocation counts to prove the short-circuit avoids re-querying. This is a specific, diff-grounded test gap for newly added caching logic, not a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Low/bug] The `permissionCacheUsage` metric semantics are corrupted in `Check`: a denial-cache hit is counted as a perm-cache hit ('true') while a genuine perm-cache hit that evaluates to deny is counted as a miss ('false'). `List` reports the same metric with correct semantics, so the cache hit-rate metric now means different things per endpoint and understates real cache effectiveness for denied traffic.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a denial-cache hit (`s.permDenialCache.Get(...)`) increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label `"true"` (cache hit) even though it is not the permission cache (`permCache`) at all. Also, when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns cached perms (`err == nil`) but `checkPermission(...)` determines `allowed == false`, the code falls through and increments `permissionCacheUsage` with `"false"` after the block, effectively counting a real permission-cache hit as a miss whenever the cached evaluation denies. In contrast, `Service.List` increments `permissionCacheUsage` based solely on whether `getCachedIdentityPermissions` hit (`err == nil`), so the metric's semantics diverge between endpoints and undercount cache effectiveness for denied checks.
